THOUGHT: This 35-year-old woman with Crohn disease treated with natalizumab for one year presents with subacute onset of gait and limb ataxia, right upper limb weakness (4/5), and a “drunken” gait — all highly suggestive of cerebellar or widespread white matter dysfunction. Natalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits α4-integrin–mediated lymphocyte trafficking across the blood–brain barrier. While effective for inflammatory bowel disease and multiple sclerosis, it carries a well-established risk of Progressive Multifocal Encephalopathy (PML), a demyelinating disease caused by reactivation of the JC virus in immunocompromised individuals. The MRI finding of lesions consistent with PML is diagnostic-confirmatory: PML typically manifests as asymmetric, non-enhancing, T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter lesions without mass effect or significant edema, often involving parieto-occipital regions but also brainstem, cerebellum, and deep white matter — which can produce ataxia, limb weakness, and gait disturbance. Her age, immunosuppressed state (due to natalizumab), clinical presentation (subacute ataxia + focal weakness), and MRI findings converge robustly on PML as the cause of her neurological decline. Other causes of ataxia (e.g., Wernicke encephalopathy, paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, MS relapse, or toxic/metabolic etiologies) are far less likely given the specific imaging finding and high-risk immunomodulatory exposure.

DIAGNOSIS: Progressive Multifocal Encephalopathy
